newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman to run for president on June 15.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman to run for president on June 15.

text.p: The Croatian government on Monday set June 15 as the date for presidential elections in which President Franjo Tudjman is likely to romp to victory for a second five-year term.
Tudjman, who will be 75 on Wednesday and is reported to be seriously ill, will run as candidate for his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party and faces little opposition.

The conservative nationalist leader, who led Croatia to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, is hugely popular in his country despite allegations of corruption and authoritarianism within the ruling party.

A statement issued at the weekend by his medical team said his health was excellent but diplomats and other independent observers say he has been battling cancer since last year and is unlikely to last another full term.

If re-elected, Tudjman will have to improve Croatia's handling of human rights issues and release the authorities' grip on the media to help the country fulfil its ambition to join West European institutions.
Talks on a cooperation agreement with the European Union have been stalled over such issues.

The United States has also pressured Croatia to hand over Croat indictees to the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague if it does not want loans from bodies such as the International Monetary Fund to be blocked.
U.S. President Bill Clinton sent a letter to Tudjman on Monday which outlined that, if conditions were met, the United States would support Croatia's integration into Western institutions.
This would include its eventual membership of NATO's Partnership for Peace military cooperation programme.

A Western diplomat said the letter, delivered to Tudjman by U.S. Ambassador Peter Galbraith, stressed Croatia would have to comply with the war crimes tribunal as well as support Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, bedrock of the U.S.-brokered 1995 Dayton peace agreement which ended the Yugoslav war.
State television trumpeted Galbraith's meeting with the president and Clinton's letter, showing file pictures of the U.S. and Croatian presidents together.
Croatia is keen to move towards the West and shake off its image as a member of the Balkans, a region it views as backward and unstable.
The top U.N. official in Croatia, Jacques Klein, slammed Tudjman last week for Zagreb's treatment of minority Serb refugees.
Tudjman will face a disunited opposition in June and there has even been suggestions of a boycott by rival parties to render hollow another victory by the president.
Liberal leader Vlado Gotovac may try the impossible and run against Tudjman but has said there is no point if the opposition does not have fair access to the media.
"This would represent fighting a battle that has already been lost," he told the independent satirical weekly Feral Tribune.
He said he would be ready to join a boycott if other candidates agreed.
Another idea being thrown around opposition circles is running a joint candidate to represent several leftist parties.
But it is believed more candidates could take some votes away from Tudjman and force him to enter a second round, only needed if he fails to secure an outright majority in the first.
